title: Nineteen Eighteen: The Pandemic Everyone Forgot

speaker.persona: Retired school nurse who volunteers with the county historical society and found her great-grandmother's 1918 letters; warm, wandering, apologetic

outlineText:
Welcome: why 1918 still matters to me
Where it started and the "Spanish flu" name [cues: Camp Funston, Kansas]
The waves
  A mild spring wave
  The deadly autumn wave
Why it was so deadly
  Young adults hit hardest
  War, crowding and pneumonia
Public health responses
  Masks and closures [cues: Philadelphia parade, St. Louis]
Aftermath
Lessons for today

segments.say: Hi everybody, thanks for coming out. I'm Maggie, I volunteer with the historical society, and before that I was a school nurse for twenty-six years, so germs are kind of my whole personality.

And the reason I give this talk is a shoebox. My great-grandmother Nell was a telephone operator in Philadelphia in nineteen eighteen, and her letters are full of who got sick at the switchboard and who didn't come back.
We found them in my aunt's attic, which also had a stuffed owl nobody in the family will admit to. It lives in my garage now. It watches me.
Nell's gonna come back later, there's one letter about a parade that still gives me chills.
Okay. So. Um, let's start at the start, I guess.

Nobody knows for sure where it came from. The first well-documented outbreak was at an army camp in Kansas that March, one cook reported sick and within days there were over a hundred men in the infirmary.

And it almost certainly didn't start in Spain. Spain was neutral in the war, so their papers weren't censored and reported it openly, even their king getting sick, so everybody else went, oh, the Spanish thing. The Spanish, of course, blamed France.
Um, sorry, hang on, I had a date written here somewhere. Never mind.
So here's what people miss, it didn't hit once and leave. It came in surges, like sets of waves at the beach, three big ones in about a year, and each one looked really different.
That first round in the spring was honestly forgettable. A few days of fever and aches, then back to work, and deaths weren't much above a normal flu season, so with a war on, nobody paid attention.
Side note, my grandson asked me if I was alive in nineteen eighteen. I'm sixty-four. I told him yes, and that I knew the Wright brothers, and he believed me.

Then late August it comes back a completely different animal, and now it's killing people. It pops up almost the same week in Boston, a port in France, and Freetown in Sierra Leone, all full of ships and soldiers.
And that fall is when it got scary. In October alone something like a hundred ninety-five thousand Americans died, the deadliest month in our history.
And remember that army cook in Kansas? A lot of folks think it was the same bug, just meaner after a summer bouncing around the camps.
Alright, so... next thing.

So what made this one such a killer? Partly it was brand new, most people's bodies had never met anything like it. Normal flu kills well under one percent of the people who catch it, this was more like two or three.
And people went downhill fast. Nurses wrote about faces turning a dusky blue as the lungs filled up, fine at breakfast and gone by the next day.
I'll get to what towns actually did about it in a bit, because some got it really right and some really didn't.

The strangest part is who it took. Usually flu is hardest on babies and grandparents. This time it was people in their twenties and thirties, healthy, strong, just starting families. Graph the deaths by age and you get a W instead of a U.
Nobody's sure why. Maybe their immune systems overreacted, sort of friendly fire. Or older folks had caught a similar strain decades earlier and kept some protection.
Um, where was I. Sorry, lost my place. Right, okay.

So what did cities do? Health departments had no vaccine, no tests, they didn't even know what caused it. So they made doctors report every case, put up cover-your-cough posters, banned spitting, and turned schools into emergency hospitals.
And with so many doctors and nurses overseas, the health boards and the Red Cross begged for anyone with training, and ordinary women, teachers, church ladies, showed up and nursed strangers.
Oh, shoot, wait, I skipped part of the why. The war! Millions of young men packed shoulder to shoulder in barracks and trenches and troop ships, the perfect setup for spreading anything.
And a lot of people actually died of the bacterial pneumonia that moved in afterward. Today that's antibiotics, but penicillin was still ten years from being discovered.
Which is partly why, like I said, the twenty-somethings got hit so hard, they were the ones crammed together.
Anyway, so, covering your face and shutting things down, that's where I was headed. San Francisco made gauze masks the law that October, and police fined people they called mask slackers.
When they brought the rule back in January, a group formed an Anti-Mask League, so that argument is over a hundred years old.

Then the famous comparison. Philadelphia went ahead with a huge war-bond parade in late September, maybe two hundred thousand people on the streets, and within about three days every hospital bed in the city was full.
St. Louis shut schools, theaters and churches and banned big gatherings early, and its death rate ended up around half of Philly's.
That's Nell's letter I promised you. She didn't go, thank goodness, but two girls from her switchboard did.
Okay, so, um, let me keep us moving... right.
When it finally burned out, around fifty million people were dead worldwide, maybe more, about six hundred seventy-five thousand here. American life expectancy dropped about twelve years in one year.
And then everybody just stopped talking about it. The war ended, the roaring twenties started, and one historian called it America's forgotten pandemic. There are hardly any monuments.
It did leave things behind. Lots of countries set up national health departments right after, Canada in nineteen nineteen, and the virus's descendants kept circulating as seasonal flu for decades.
I'll come back to what that means for us at the very end.
Alright, um, last thing.
So what do I hope you take home? That the boring stuff works. Cities that moved early, stacked measures together, and kept at it did better. San Francisco eased up too soon and got a second spike.
And honesty. Plenty of officials downplayed it for wartime morale, called it ordinary grippe, and people stopped trusting anything they heard. Being straight with people matters.
And we've got things Nell never had, vaccines, antibiotics, oxygen. So thank you, and go ask your great-aunt what's in her attic.
